concept_summary: Einstein's 1905 analysis shows that a small sphere suspended in a stationary liquid is buffeted by molecular-kinetic fluctuations, so its displacement is random rather than deterministic. The diffusion coefficient D = (R*T/N)/(6*pi*k*P) depends on absolute temperature, the liquid's viscosity, and the sphere's radius. The observable consequence is a mean-square displacement along one axis that grows linearly with elapsed time, so the one-axis root-mean-square displacement grows as the square root of time. This lesson computes D, MSD = 2*D*t, and RMS = sqrt(2*D*t) in micrometre-based units and lets you vary T, eta, a, and t.

controls.label: Absolute temperature T
controls.meaning: Temperature in kelvin; D is proportional to T, so raising T raises D and RMS.

controls.label: Dynamic viscosity eta
controls.meaning: Liquid viscosity in mPa*s; D is inversely proportional to eta, so raising eta lowers D and RMS.

controls.label: Particle radius a
controls.meaning: Sphere radius in micrometres; D is inversely proportional to a, so larger particles diffuse more slowly.

controls.label: Elapsed time t
controls.meaning: Observation time in seconds; MSD grows linearly with t and RMS grows as sqrt(t).

equations.explanation: Einstein's diffusion expression in the paper's symbols: R is the gas constant, T absolute temperature, N Avogadro's number, k the liquid's viscosity coefficient, and P the sphere's radius. The source excerpt supplies this as a transcription of Section 3.

Teaching conversion to convenient units: replace R/N by the modern Boltzmann constant k_B = 1.380649e-23 J/K, write eta for viscosity in mPa*s and a for radius in micrometres, and convert SI factors so D comes out in micrometres squared per second. The decimal coefficient 0.01380649 and the pi approximation are modern unit-conversion artifacts, not numbers fitted by Einstein.

Equation (11) of Section 4 defines lambda_x as the square root of the arithmetic mean of squared displacements along the x-axis. The mean-square displacement is 2*D*t, so the one-axis RMS is its square root.
Because RMS = sqrt(2*D*t), quadrupling t multiplies RMS by sqrt(4) = 2. The source states the mean displacement is proportional to the square root of the time.

explanation_steps.heading: Diffusion coefficient from molecular-kinetic theory
explanation_steps.body: A small sphere in a stationary liquid is hit by molecular-kinetic fluctuations, so its motion is random. Einstein's Section 3 expression D = (R*T/N)/(6*pi*k*P) ties the diffusion coefficient to temperature, the liquid's viscosity coefficient k, and the sphere's radius P.

explanation_steps.heading: Converted working expression
explanation_steps.body: For convenient micrometre-scale numbers we convert to D = 0.01380649*T/(6*pi*eta*a), with T in K, eta in mPa*s, a in micrometres, and D in micrometres squared per second. The coefficient 0.01380649 and the pi approximation are modern unit conversions, not values fitted by Einstein.

explanation_steps.heading: From mean-square displacement to one-axis RMS
explanation_steps.body: Section 4, equation (11) gives lambda_x = sqrt(mean(x^2)) = sqrt(2*D*t). The mean-square displacement along one axis is 2*D*t, and its square root is the one-axis RMS. Because the source notes the mean displacement is proportional to the square root of the time, quadrupling t doubles RMS.

explorations.change: Set t = 0 s while keeping T = 300 K, eta = 1 mPa*s, and a = 1 um.
explorations.observe: MSD and RMS both become exactly 0, while D remains 0.000732 um^2/s.
explorations.why: MSD = 2*D*t and RMS = sqrt(2*D*t) both contain a factor t, so they vanish at t = 0; D itself does not depend on t, so it stays positive.

explorations.change: Quadruple t from 1 s to 4 s at fixed T = 300 K, eta = 1 mPa*s, a = 1 um.
explorations.observe: MSD grows by a factor of 4, from 0.001464 to 0.005856 um^2, while RMS grows only by a factor of 2, from 0.038262 to 0.076524 um.
explorations.why: MSD is linear in t, but RMS = sqrt(2*D*t) is proportional to sqrt(t); the source states the mean displacement is proportional to the square root of the time.

explorations.change: Double eta from 1 to 2 mPa*s, or double a from 1 to 2 um, at fixed T = 300 K and t = 1 s.
explorations.observe: D halves from 0.000732 to 0.000366 um^2/s, and RMS falls from 0.038262 to 0.027055 um.
explorations.why: D is inversely proportional to both eta and a, so doubling either denominator factor halves D and reduces RMS by sqrt(2).

grounding.paper_title: On the Movement of Small Particles Suspended in a Stationary Liquid Demanded by the Molecular-Kinetic Theory of Heat (1905)

source_claims.claim: Einstein's Section 3 gives the diffusion coefficient of a spherical particle in terms of temperature, Avogadro's number, the liquid's viscosity coefficient, and the sphere's radius.
source_claims.locator: Section 3, printed page 12 (PDF page 8), equation transcription

source_claims.claim: Section 4, equation (11) defines the one-axis root-mean-square displacement as the square root of the arithmetic mean of squared x-displacements, equal to sqrt(2*D*t).
source_claims.locator: Section 4, equation (11), printed page 17 (PDF page 10), equation transcription

source_claims.claim: The mean displacement grows as the square root of the elapsed time.
source_claims.quote: The mean displacement is therefore proportional to the square root of the time.

teaching_simplifications: The decimal coefficient 0.01380649 and the pi approximation 3.141592653589793 are modern unit-conversion artifacts, not numbers fitted by Einstein.
The modern Boltzmann constant k_B = 1.380649e-23 J/K is supplied from NIST and is not quoted from the 1905 paper.
Writing eta for viscosity and a for radius, and expressing D in micrometres squared per second, is a teaching notation and unit choice.
All slider values are teaching examples, not reproductions of any measurement or experimental result.
The line view sweeps t for RMS at the current T, eta, and a; it is a toy demonstration of the scaling relation, not a simulated particle trajectory.

limitations: This lesson computes the ensemble mean-square and root-mean-square displacement; it does not simulate a deterministic particle trajectory.
RMS is not the mean signed displacement, the mean absolute displacement, the total path length, or the three-dimensional RMS displacement.
The converted expression uses a modern Boltzmann constant and unit conversions that are not part of the 1905 paper's original symbols.
The slider ranges and default values are teaching choices, not experimental conditions from the source.
The line view is a toy scaling demonstration and does not reproduce any measured data.

title: Einstein 1905: Diffusion and One-Axis RMS Displacement of a Small Sphere

visualizations.title: One-axis RMS displacement vs elapsed time

why_it_matters: Einstein's result connects an observable, random-looking displacement of a microscopic particle to molecular-kinetic theory. It shows that measuring D, together with T, eta, and a, gives a route to Avogadro's number and to testing the kinetic theory of heat. The square-root-of-time scaling is a signature of diffusive spreading: quadrupling the observation time only doubles the typical one-axis displacement, so RMS is not a speed and not a deterministic path length.
